changelog_text:
A shared world for Kitten Space Agency: several players, each in their own game, flying in
one universe kept by a dedicated server that runs on Linux with no game installed.

Everyone in a world needs **KSA `2026.11.10.5801`** and a mod of this release. A game and a
server speaking different versions refuse each other by name rather than misread the
bytes, and this one speaks **protocol 23**.

## What's new

The Multiplayer window is laid out to a design by Beik, and it says what is the
server's apart from what is yours.

The list is the window. Every column holds a fact about a server -- its name,
who is on it, the world it holds, the round trip to it -- so the world it holds
stays on the row even when something about it is wrong, which is exactly when
you want to compare one server against another. Whether your game can join is
the state of the row instead: a server you cannot join carries a word beside its
name saying which of the things that must match did not, and the sentence
telling you what to do about it sits beside the button that would act on it.

PLAY ALONE is in the title bar, in the colour of something worth pressing.
CONNECT is at the foot of the block that says where you are going and what it
wants, and is greyed where that server would turn you away over its build or
your mods -- not where it is merely full or did not answer, since the first
changes while you look at it and the second is as likely to be a lost datagram.
Under the list, what you are on the left and where you are going on the right.

A server that would refuse you now says so in the window. It used to say it only
in the log and the chat, so pressing CONNECT looked like pressing nothing. The
list also weighed only mods you were missing and not mods you were running that
a world has not got -- which a server refuses just as firmly -- so it would call
a server joinable and then go quiet when it was not. A server that wants no
password says so in words rather than by grey.

The window opens on the monitor the game is on, which it did not when there was
more than one. The scoreboard sizes its own columns, so a long name no longer
runs under the ping beside it. The badge in the menu bar says "connecting..."
while it is.

Nothing in the protocol changed: 0.15 and 0.16 games speak version 23 and can
play together.

<details>
<summary>Every change since v0.15.0</summary>

- docs: the window's design is Beik's, and the README says so
- fix(mod): the blocks are a step above the body, not three steps
- feat(mod): the start-settings box moves into the block it is about
- fix(mod): room between the words and the rules, and a block that does not scroll
- fix(mod): the Latency column ends where the button under it begins, and Add server goes
- feat(mod): PLAY ALONE sits in the titlebar
- fix(mod): the list fills its box and the blocks under it are blocks
- feat(mod): the start window is the list, with what you are and where you are going under it
- fix(mod): a server says whether it wants a password, and a chosen row still reads
</details>

## Playing

Install [StarMap](https://github.com/StarMapLoader/StarMap), unzip `KSAMultiplayer-*.zip`
into KSA's `mods` folder and enable it. Load a world, get into flight, and the
**Multiplayer** window is at the top right.

There is a server at **`mp.ksarmory.com`** to try it on.

Hold **Tab** for who is playing and their ping, **Enter** for a chat line. A craft someone
else is flying carries their name and is theirs: you can watch it, not fly it. Changing the
simulation speed is put to everyone first, and only whoever asked can end the warp.

## Hosting

```bash
docker run -dit --name ksamp -p 50100:50100/udp -v ksamp-world:/data \
    -e KSAMP_NAME="My server" ghcr.io/laurensdev/ksamp-server@sha256:4dc3bb720ab832bead22cb6e4ddd09e8527ef558f5eb4423773dd8a6743b97c6
```

Or an executable from below, needing no .NET and no KSA:
`ksamp-server-linux-x64.tar.gz` (with a systemd unit beside it),
`ksamp-server-linux-arm64.tar.gz` for a Pi or an ARM VPS, or
`ksamp-server-win-x64.zip` to run `ksamp-server.exe` on the machine you already have.
The server has no world until a player gives it one, and hands that world to everyone who
joins after -- or set `empty-world` and it starts with one of its own.

Hosting on the same machine you play on works: the server is its own process and needs no
game. Whoever else joins needs the port open to them.

Its commands are typed into its console, which is standard input -- hence `-it` above, and
`docker attach ksamp` to reach it, Ctrl+P Ctrl+Q to leave it running. `clear` is the broom
for a world filling up with spent stages: every craft nobody is flying goes, out of every
game and not just out of the server, and `clear Rocket_*` narrows it. `reload` hands the
world out again, which takes a few seconds and no reconnection, and is the only thing that
ever puts universe time back.

## Upgrading a server when KSA has

A world remembers the KSA build of whoever gave it to the server, and the server turns away
anyone running a different one. So the day KSA updates, a world seeded before it refuses
**everybody who updates** -- and nothing says so from inside the game beyond the refusal.
Either `fresh` at the console, which throws that world away and starts an empty one, or
`set ksa-build <the new build>` to make the operator's word the test instead of the
world's. A world the server started by itself records no build and turns nobody away.

## State

Two games on one machine have flown in one world through it: launching, EVA, chat, the
scoreboard, nametags, a voted time warp, and an 89-part rocket staged while the other game
watched and rebuilt the stage it dropped. Another player's engines are seen to burn even on
a craft this game is not simulating, 7,576 km away. What two games across the internet do
is not known yet.

listing.description:
A shared world for **Kitten Space Agency**: several players, each in their own game, flying in one universe kept by a **dedicated server**. The server runs on Linux, Windows or a Raspberry Pi, needs no copy of the game, and holds the world whether anybody is playing or not.

Any craft syncs: rockets, rovers, kittens walking about on EVA. You see other players fly, stage, burn and crash in real time, each craft carrying its owner's name.

### Playing together

- **A craft is its owner's.** You can watch one somebody else is flying, ride along with it, and see its engines burn — but not take it, board it or empty it out. When its owner leaves, it comes free.
- **One clock.** Everybody keeps the server's time. A game that falls behind catches up on its own, and nobody is left watching a world minutes out of date.
- **Time warp is asked, not taken.** Changing the simulation speed is put to the room first, and only whoever asked can end it. A game that cannot keep up holds the speed down for everyone, so nothing runs away from the slowest machine.
- **Hold Tab** for who is playing and their ping, **Enter** for a chat line.
- Launchpads are shared out, so two players launching at one site do not land on top of each other.

### The server

One self-contained executable. Point it at a port and it waits; the first player to join gives it their world, and it hands that world to everyone who joins after. Or set `empty-world` and it starts with an empty one of its own, so nobody has to seed it.

It keeps the world between runs, saves periodically, and has a console: `clear` sweeps up the spent stages a shared world fills with, `reload` hands the world out again without anybody reconnecting, and `fresh` throws it away and starts over. Players can be made admins and run those commands from inside the game.

There is a server at **`mp.ksarmory.com`** to try it on.

### What you need

Everyone in a world needs **the same KSA build**, the same mod version, and every mod the world's craft use. The server turns away anyone who differs and says what is missing, rather than letting a mismatch corrupt the world quietly.

### Honest status

Two games on one machine have flown in one world through all of this: launching, EVA, chat, nametags, a voted warp, and an 89-part rocket staged while the other game watched and rebuilt the dropped stage as its own craft. Another player's engines are seen to burn even on a craft your game is not simulating, thousands of kilometres away.

What a dozen players across the internet do to it is not known yet. Bug reports are welcome.
